clinicalPearls: SPG52 is an autosomal recessive complicated hereditary spastic paraplegia caused by biallelic variants in AP4S1, which encodes the small sigma-4 subunit of the heterotetrameric adaptor protein complex 4 (AP-4); it is one of the four AP-4-deficiency spastic paraplegias.

The AP-4-deficiency phenotype is stereotyped: early hypotonia in infancy that evolves into progressive spastic paraplegia or tetraplegia, so the initial picture can mimic hypotonic then spastic cerebral palsy.
Severe global developmental delay and intellectual disability with absent or minimal speech is typical.
Postnatal (acquired) microcephaly, epilepsy or febrile seizures, and a characteristically cheerful demeanour with stereotypic laughter are recognised clues.
MRI commonly shows a thin corpus callosum, reduced white-matter volume and ventricular enlargement.
The four AP-4 subunits are clinically indistinguishable: AP4B1 (SPG47), AP4M1 (SPG50), AP4E1 (SPG51) and AP4S1 (SPG52) cause the same syndrome, so genotype rather than phenotype defines the subtype.
Mechanistically, AP-4 loss mislocalises the autophagy protein ATG9A, placing SPG52 among the autophagy-related HSPs.

Care is supportive, addressing spasticity, seizures, and developmental and orthopaedic needs; no disease-modifying therapy is established, though the shared mechanism has prompted interest in unified AP-4 therapeutic approaches.
reference.pathophysiology: SPG52 is an autosomal recessive complicated hereditary spastic paraplegia caused by biallelic loss-of-function variants in AP4S1, which encodes the small sigma-4 subunit of adaptor protein complex 4 (AP-4). AP-4 is a heterotetramer of the subunits epsilon, beta-4, mu-4 and sigma-4 that assembles at the trans-Golgi network and mediates the sorting and vesicular export of selected transmembrane cargoes; a key cargo is the autophagy-related transmembrane protein ATG9A, and AP-4 also participates in delivering receptors such as AMPA-type glutamate receptors to the somatodendritic compartment of neurons. Loss of any single subunit destabilises the whole complex, so AP4S1 defects cause the same AP-4-deficiency syndrome as AP4B1 (SPG47), AP4M1 (SPG50) and AP4E1 (SPG51). The resulting mistrafficking and trans-Golgi and cytoplasmic retention of ATG9A impairs autophagosome formation and axonal homeostasis, driving corticospinal degeneration with spasticity together with a severe neurodevelopmental phenotype of intellectual disability, acquired microcephaly and seizures.
additionalDifferentials: The allelic AP-4-deficiency HSPs SPG47 (AP4B1), SPG50 (AP4M1) and SPG51 (AP4E1) - clinically identical and distinguished only by the gene involved
SPG45 (NT5C2) and SPG49 (TECPR2) - other recessive complicated childhood HSPs with intellectual disability
SPG11 (spatacsin) and SPG15 (ZFYVE26) - recessive HSP with thin corpus callosum
Spastic or dyskinetic cerebral palsy - the key mimic in early childhood
Angelman syndrome, given the cheerful demeanour with stereotypic laughter, developmental delay and seizures
Leukodystrophies and other neurodevelopmental disorders with a thin corpus callosum
additionalInvestigations: Molecular testing (exome sequencing or HSP and neurodevelopmental panel) for biallelic AP4S1 variants
MRI of the brain (thin corpus callosum, white-matter loss and ventriculomegaly; assess the head-size trajectory)
Orthopaedic assessment for contractures and foot deformity, with hip surveillance
Parental testing and segregation analysis to confirm recessive inheritance
redFlags: Rapidly progressive contractures or hip subluxation compromising positioning and care
Emergence of severe spasticity replacing early hypotonia and limiting mobility
reference.prognosis: SPG52 causes lifelong severe disability with intellectual impairment and progressive spasticity; most affected individuals do not achieve independent walking or fluent speech, although life expectancy can extend into adulthood with good supportive care.
pitfalls: Diagnosing cerebral palsy in a hypotonic infant who later develops spasticity and missing the genetic diagnosis and its recurrence risk.
Expecting the phenotype to distinguish the AP-4 subtypes - only genetic testing separates SPG47, SPG50, SPG51 and SPG52.
Under-recognising the cheerful demeanour with stereotypic laughter as a diagnostic clue.
Overlooking recurrence-risk counselling in consanguineous families.
references: Standard clinical neurology and neurogenetics reference texts
Peer-reviewed reviews on the classification and genetics of hereditary spastic paraplegia
Curated hereditary spastic paraplegia gene and phenotype resources
management: Symptomatic antispasticity therapy with baclofen or tizanidine, escalating to intrathecal baclofen for severe spasticity, plus botulinum toxin for focal spasticity
Anti-seizure medication for epilepsy, with prompt antipyretic management given febrile-triggered seizures
Physiotherapy, stretching, supportive seating and orthoses, with orthopaedic care for contractures and foot deformity and hip surveillance
Developmental, educational and communication support including augmentative and alternative communication for severe intellectual disability and minimal speech
Feeding and swallowing assessment with nutritional support
Genetic counselling for autosomal recessive inheritance and carrier testing of relatives
Multidisciplinary paediatric neurology, rehabilitation and complex-care input
